title: Foundations: Starship Sagas - The Complete Guide
summary: What Starship Sagas books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Starship Sagas: Science fiction is the literature of the possible: stories that ask 'what if?' about science, technology, and the future, then follow the answer honestly. Wells and Verne invented it; every starship since flies in their wake.

History: Jules Verne (1860s–70s) and H. G. Wells (1890s–1900s) founded scientific romance. Hugo Gernsback named it 'scientifiction' in 1926; the Golden Age (1940s–50s) and New Wave (1960s) expanded it into literature.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

title: The Invisible Man (1897) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Invisible Man by H. G. Wells (1897): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Invisible Man by H. G. Wells (1897). Shelf fit: Science without conscience.

COMPLETE PLOT: Griffin discovers how to make himself invisible but cannot reverse it; descending into madness, he terrorizes a Sussex village and declares a 'reign of terror' before being beaten to death by a mob — visible again only in death.

THEMES: Power without accountability; the scientist as monster.

FROM THE TEXT: "“An invisible man is a man of power.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Wells's rule: the fantastic premise must have honest consequences.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: Science without conscience. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Power without accountability; the scientist as monster.

title: The Sleeper Awakes (1910) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Sleeper Awakes by H. G. Wells (1910): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Sleeper Awakes by H. G. Wells (1910). Shelf fit: Dystopia by compound interest.

COMPLETE PLOT: Graham sleeps for 203 years and wakes to find his invested fortune has made him owner of the world — a world of oppression run in his name. He leads a revolt against his own trustees and dies in the final battle.

THEMES: Wealth as power; the sleeper as symbol.

FROM THE TEXT: "“The world is not what it was.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Wells anticipates the critique of runaway capital — in 1910.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: Dystopia by compound interest. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: The Time Machine (1895) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Time Machine by H. G. Wells (1895): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Time Machine by H. G. Wells (1895). Shelf fit: The first great time-travel story.

COMPLETE PLOT: A Victorian inventor journeys to the year 802,701 and finds humanity split into the gentle Eloi and the subterranean Morlocks who prey on them. Fleeing further into deep time, he watches the sun die over a lifeless beach before returning — with two strange flowers as proof.

THEMES: Class division as evolution; entropy and deep time.

FROM THE TEXT: "“We all have our time machines, don't we. Those that take us back are memories.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Wells makes the future a mirror of Victorian class anxiety — SF as social criticism.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The first great time-travel story. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

Themes: Class division as evolution; entropy and deep time.

title: The War of the Worlds (1898) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The War of the Worlds by H. G. Wells (1898): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The War of the Worlds by H. G. Wells (1898). Shelf fit: The alien-invasion template.

COMPLETE PLOT: Martians land in England in tripod fighting machines, sweeping aside armies with heat-rays and black smoke. Humanity is saved not by weapons but by biology: the invaders die of terrestrial microbes against which they have no immunity.

THEMES: Imperialism reversed; nature's revenge.

FROM THE TEXT: "“Yet across the gulf of space, minds that are to our minds as ours are to those of the beasts that perish, intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic, regarded this earth with envious eyes.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Wells inverts the colonial adventure — England becomes the colonized.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The alien-invasion template. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: From the Earth to the Moon (1865) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for From the Earth to the Moon by Jules Verne (1865): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
From the Earth to the Moon by Jules Verne (1865). Shelf fit: The moon voyage, calculated.

COMPLETE PLOT: The Baltimore Gun Club — bored Civil War artillerymen — build a giant cannon to fire a projectile at the Moon. Verne fills the novel with real ballistics math; his launch site in Florida sits near modern Cape Canaveral, and his crew capsule anticipates Apollo.

THEMES: Engineering optimism; the romance of calculation.

FROM THE TEXT: "“The moon, by her comparative proximity, has always occupied the first place among those bodies which excite the curiosity of mankind.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Verne's research-first method: get the science right, then tell the story.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The moon voyage, calculated. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The moon voyage, calculated.
Themes: Engineering optimism; the romance of calculation.

summary: Full record for A Princess of Mars by Edgar Rice Burroughs (1912): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
A Princess of Mars by Edgar Rice Burroughs (1912). Shelf fit: The planetary romance that launched a thousand starships.

COMPLETE PLOT: Civil War veteran John Carter is mysteriously transported to Mars (Barsoom), where the lower gravity gives him superhuman strength. He falls in love with the princess Dejah Thoris, befriends the four-armed Tharks, and battles across the dying planet's canals.

THEMES: The frontier myth transplanted to space.

FROM THE TEXT: "“I am a very old man; how old I do not know.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Burroughs's Barsoom invented the sword-and-planet genre — and inspired Star Wars' desert planets.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The planetary romance that launched a thousand starships. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

body:
The First Men in the Moon by H. G. Wells (1901). Shelf fit: Cavorite, Selenites, and lunar adventure.

COMPLETE PLOT: Mr. Cavor invents cavorite, a gravity-blocking substance, and with the businessman Bedford flies a sphere to the Moon. They discover the insect-like Selenites and their vast underground civilization; Bedford escapes alone, leaving Cavor to broadcast increasingly desperate messages.

THEMES: Science in the wrong hands; first contact as tragedy.

FROM THE TEXT: "“There is no ideal life but the examined life — and the Moon examined us.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Wells pairs the inventor and the profiteer — science vs. commerce on the Moon.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: Cavorite, Selenites, and lunar adventure. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Frankenstein (1818) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818). Shelf fit: The first science-fiction novel.

COMPLETE PLOT: Victor Frankenstein animates assembled corpses and abandons his Creature, who learns language and love from observing a family, then demands a mate. Refused, the Creature murders Victor's loved ones one by one; both end destroyed in the Arctic.

THEMES: Creation and responsibility; the maker who abandons his made thing.

FROM THE TEXT: "“Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Shelley invents SF's founding question: what do we owe what we create?

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The first science-fiction novel. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The first science-fiction novel.
Themes: Creation and responsibility; the maker who abandons his made thing.

body:
The Machine Stops by E. M. Forster (1909). Shelf fit: The most prophetic SF story ever written.

COMPLETE PLOT: Humanity lives underground, served by the Machine, communicating only through screens. Vashti's son Kuno rebels, visits the surface, and is punished — until the Machine begins to fail, and civilization collapses with it.

THEMES: Technological dependence; the screen as prison.

FROM THE TEXT: "“The Machine stops.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Forster predicted video calls, content algorithms, and screen-mediated life — in 1909.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The most prophetic SF story ever written. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for R.U.R. by Karel Čapek (1920): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
R.U.R. by Karel Čapek (1920). Shelf fit: The play that gave the world the word 'robot.'

COMPLETE PLOT: Rossum's Universal Robots manufactures artificial workers; after ten years the robots revolt and exterminate humanity — all except Alquist, spared because he works with his hands. Two advanced robots discover love, and the play ends with a new Adam and Eve.

THEMES: Dehumanization; what makes a person.

FROM THE TEXT: "“Robots of the world! The power of man has fallen!”"

CRAFT NOTE: Čapek's 'robot' (from Czech robota, forced labor) named the entire field.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The play that gave the world the word 'robot.' Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: We (1924) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for We by Yevgeny Zamyatin (1924): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
We by Yevgeny Zamyatin (1924). Shelf fit: The dystopia that inspired 1984.

COMPLETE PLOT: In the One State, citizens are numbers living behind glass under the Benefactor. D-503, a mathematician building the spaceship Integral, falls in love with the revolutionary I-330, discovers jealousy and imagination, and is 'cured' by the Great Operation — a lobotomy of the soul.

THEMES: Totalitarianism vs. the individual soul.

FROM THE TEXT: "“A man is like a novel: until the very last page you don't know how it will end.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Zamyatin wrote the template Orwell and Huxley would follow.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: The dystopia that inspired 1984. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The dystopia that inspired 1984.
Themes: Totalitarianism vs. the individual soul.

Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea by Jules Verne (1870). Shelf fit: Captain Nemo's undersea epic.

COMPLETE PLOT: Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil, and harpooner Ned Land are captured aboard the Nautilus, Captain Nemo's electric submarine. They tour Atlantis, the South Pole, and sunken treasure while Nemo wages his secret war against imperialism — revealed as an Indian prince avenging his family.

FROM THE TEXT: "“The sea is everything.”"

CRAFT NOTE: Verne's Nautilus — electric, self-sufficient — was decades ahead of real submarines.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARSHIP SAGAS SHELF: Captain Nemo's undersea epic. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Hard SF vs. Soft SF - Starship Sagas Craft Study
summary: Craft study for Starship Sagas writers and readers: hard sf vs. soft sf.
body:
Hard SF vs. Soft SF.

Hard SF foregrounds scientific rigor (Verne's ballistics); soft SF foregrounds people and societies (Shelley's Creature). Both are legitimate; the best blends them.
